chunks: From him, from Abdullah ibn Amir, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Uqbah ibn Muslim and Ammar ibn Marwan, from Salamah ibn Muhrij, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man died, and he has wealth with me, and he has a daughter, and he has mawali (clients/freemen). He said to me: 'Go and give the daughter half, and withhold the remainder.' When I returned, I informed our companions of this, and they said: 'He gave you from the Bag of Light.' I returned to him and said: 'Indeed, our companions said: He gave you from the Bag of Light.' He said: 'Did anyone know that he gave you from the Bag of Light?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'Then go and give the daughter the remainder.'

key_terms.النِّصْفَ: Half (the initial portion allocated to the daughter)
key_terms.الْبَاقِيَ: The remainder (the second portion allocated after clarification)
key_terms.جِرَابُ النُّورَةِ: The Bag of Light (a metaphorical term for the Imam's exclusive knowledge or treasury)
key_terms.مَوَالِي: Mawali (clients or freedmen, often considered extended family in inheritance law)

ai.seo_question: How is a deceased person's debt distributed among heirs according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the principle of *Ihtiyat* (prudence) and the Imam's exclusive authority in resolving ambiguous inheritance cases, specifically regarding the interplay between the daughter and the *Mawali* (clients). The reference to *Jirab al-Nur* (Bag of Light) signifies the Imam's unique, divinely-inspired knowledge or treasury, which allows him to adjust distributions based on hidden circumstances or superior wisdom. This highlights the Shia scholarly view that the Imam’s directive can supersede standard fixed shares when necessary to ensure justice or account for unrecorded obligations.
